messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Mark, a 50-year-old European American psychologist, has been struggling with profound distress following a traumatic event that occurred several months ago. Mark’s life was once defined by his professional achievements and personal relationships; however, the experience of being raped has fundamentally altered his sense of self and daily functioning. The trauma has left Mark with intense triggers that have become deeply ingrained in his daily life. The smell of alcohol, often encountered at social gatherings or when colleagues celebrate a milestone at work, sets off a chain reaction within him. He finds himself pushing the memory away before he can fully recall it, as though the full recollection is too much to bear. This olfactory trigger not only sparks vivid sensations but also plunges him into emotional numbness and a feeling of dehumanization. When sirens blare in the distance, another trigger that he often encounters while driving or walking through the city, he becomes acutely aware of his own vulnerability, further cementing his belief that he is no longer capable of doing the things that once defined him as a person. Mark’s experience with memory is fragmented and intense. He can’t seem to put the frightening event into words; it feels too chaotic and overwhelming. Sometimes he experiences the full emotional intensity of the trauma without any clear image or memory, which leaves him feeling disconnected from his surroundings. This disconnect has led Mark to push away his emotions and memories, making it even more difficult for him to process what happened. The more he avoids these feelings and recollections, the stronger his negative appraisals become. He feels dead inside, certain that he can no longer perform at work or fulfill the roles he once took pride in. The cycle perpetuates itself; Mark’s triggers lead to profound emotional numbness and a sense of dehumanization, which further disrupts his memory processes. The inability to fully engage with his memories only reinforces his negative appraisals, creating a self-reinforcing loop that continues to tighten around him. This loop has had concrete consequences in both his personal and professional life. For instance, at work, the lingering smell of alcohol from client meetings often disrupts Mark’s concentration, leading to errors or miscommunications with clients. In his personal life, he avoids social gatherings altogether, isolating himself from friends and family who might otherwise provide support. His wife has noticed a significant change in him; she feels that her husband is no longer present in their relationship, further compounding the emotional toll on both of them. The weight of these experiences finally brought Mark to seek help. He is most afraid that he will never be able to reclaim his former self and that the trauma will define the rest of his life. However, he is also hopeful that with therapy, he can start to process his memories more effectively and regain a sense of capability and connection in both his personal and professional spheres. In this current state, Mark’s journey towards recovery is fraught but not without hope. The tightening loop of triggers, negative appraisals, and disrupted memory processes underscores the complexity of his experience, yet it also highlights the critical need for intervention to break these cycles and restore a sense of self.
